rationale: I'm adding per-site centring of each protein. The four CSF cohorts were collected and run separately, so each protein's baseline level can shift from cohort to cohort, and an L2-regularised linear model may pick those shifts up instead of disease signal. In `featurize`, each protein's log2 site median is subtracted and the overall median added back, which lines the four cohorts up. This uses only the `site` metadata, never labels. One risk: if the share of AD cases differs a lot between sites, this centring will also remove some real disease signal.

I'm adding a second, small logistic model built on a prior-biology CSF panel of about 30 proteins and averaging its probabilities with the whole-proteome model. The panel covers tau, the 14-3-3 family, SMOC1, neurofilament, glial markers, synaptic proteins and the glycolytic proteins from Bader et al. 2020. The panel is fixed in advance and never uses labels, so it gives a strong, stable signal that doesn't depend on picking features from a small sample. That should reduce the variance of the 1,500-feature L2 model at n≈110.

I'm adding standardized age as a covariate to the prior-biology panel model, with missing ages filled by the training-fold median. Age is the strongest known risk factor for clinical AD, and the clinical non-AD groups in these memory-clinic cohorts tend to be younger, so age should add signal that the CSF proteins don't fully carry. This uses only non-label metadata.

I'm adding a third ensemble member: an equal-weight composite of the prior-biology panel proteins. Each protein is standardised, gets weight ±1 by the sign of its training-fold correlation with the label (proteins with |r| < 0.1 are dropped), and the score is turned into a probability with a 2-parameter logistic fit. At n≈110, fitting one weight per protein is noisy, while equal-weight sign scores are known to be more stable; this should cut the variance of the panel signal without losing direction.

CSF proteins quantified in only 20–80% of training samples are dropped from the whole-proteome model today. Many of these are low-abundance, brain-derived proteins (synaptic, neuronal, glial), and because missingness follows abundance, whether a protein is detected at all tracks its level and could carry disease signal. This change adds binary "detected" indicators for those proteins to the whole-proteome L2 model; the intensity features and the panel model stay as they are.

Both logistic models currently use fixed regularization strengths (C=0.05 for the whole proteome, C=0.1 for the panel). The best amount of shrinkage at n≈110 depends a lot on how many features each model has and how strong their signal is, so I'm choosing each model's C by nested grouped 5-fold CV inside the training fold, using pooled out-of-fold AUROC and `groups_train` for grouping. No outer labels are used.

Right now each sample is centred on the median of whatever proteins were quantified in it. Missing values tend to be the low-abundance proteins, so samples with more missing values get a higher median and a biased offset. I'll compute each sample's median only over a fixed set of proteins quantified in every sample (label-free; falls back to ≥90% detection if fewer than 50 qualify), so normalization uses the same protein set for everyone.

Blood contamination during lumbar puncture varies by sample and by cohort, and it raises erythrocyte proteins (haemoglobins, CA1, PRDX2, CAT, …) plus anything that co-varies with them. That is a non-disease source of variance in both models. In `featurize` I'll build a label-free per-sample erythrocyte-contamination score and regress it out of every protein that tracks it (|r| ≥ 0.2), so the classifiers see brain-derived signal rather than how bloody the tap was.

The biggest gain so far (round 8) came from removing variation caused by blood contamination. Geyer et al. 2019 describe two more contamination signals with their own marker sets: platelet contamination (PF4, PPBP, TLN1, MYL9, …) and partial clotting of the sample (fibrinogens FGA, FGB, FGG). This change regresses those two scores out as well, one after the other, using the same label-free method as round 8, so neither classifier learns from how each sample was handled.

After erythrocyte, platelet and coagulation removal, the next big non-disease source of variance in CSF is how much plasma protein leaks across the blood–CSF barrier. This leakage, measured clinically as the albumin quotient, depends on age, CSF flow and vascular factors, and it moves hundreds of plasma-derived proteins together. I'm adding a fourth label-free axis: a score built from liver-made plasma proteins that the brain doesn't produce (ALB, AHSG, APOA1/A2/B/H, HRG, ITIH1/2, F2, PLG, SERPINC1, KNG1, …). It is regressed out with the same procedure as the other contamination axes, so the classifiers see brain-derived signal instead of barrier leakiness.

This round extends the prior-biology panel with two CSF modules from Higginbotham et al. 2020 / Johnson et al. 2020. The first is the glycolytic proteins that rise in clinical AD (LDHA, GAPDH, PGK1, TPI1, PGAM1, MIF). The second is the neuronal-pentraxin and secretory-granule proteins that fall in AD but much less in other dementias (NPTX1, NPTXR, SCG2, PCSK1, PCSK1N, CHGA, CHGB). The idea is that the panel model, which needs few features and gives a stable signal, should separate clinical AD from clinical non-AD better than the current Bader-only list.

I'm adding a third ensemble member: a single fixed-direction log-ratio score, fed through a 1-feature logistic fit and averaged in with equal weight. The score is mean z of AD-elevated proteins (YWHAG, SMOC1) minus mean z of synaptic proteins that fall in AD (NPTX2, NPTX1, NPTXR, VGF), following the CSF YWHAG:NPTX2 ratio of Oh et al. 2025. Unlike round 4, the signs come from prior biology, not training labels. Synaptic loss relative to neuronal-injury and 14-3-3 release should be specific to clinical AD over other diagnoses, and a hand-built contrast is much less noisy at n≈110 than letting L2 learn those weights.

Round 12 showed that a hand-built score with signs fixed by biology is more stable at n≈110 than letting L2 learn the weights. This change adds a fourth equal-weight member built the same way from a different pathway: the mean z of the CSF glycolysis module, which rises in AD (Bader 2020; Higginbotham/Johnson 2020: PKM, ALDOA, ENO1, GAPDH, LDHA, PGK1, TPI1, PGAM1), minus the mean z of the neuroendocrine secretory-granule module, which falls in AD (SCG2, PCSK1, PCSK1N, CHGA, CHGB). Glial and metabolic activation relative to neuronal secretory loss should separate clinical AD from other diagnoses independently of the 14-3-3 vs pentraxin contrast.

The ensemble's fixed-direction members cover tau, neurodegeneration and synapses (14-3-3/SMOC1 vs pentraxins; glycolysis vs secretory granules), but nothing tracks amyloid, the pathology that defines AD. I'm adding a fifth equal-weight member: the mean z of the amyloid-associated matrisome module, whose signs are fixed in advance as rising in AD (SMOC1, SPON1, MDK, NTN1, SLIT2, HTRA1, OLFML3, FRZB, CTHRC1, COL25A1; Johnson et al. 2022 M42 / Bai 2020). It should help separate clinical AD from non-AD dementias that have tau or neurodegeneration changes without amyloid.

DIA intensities have heavy tails: single-sample interference, misidentified peptides, and imputed half-minimum values on proteins detected in 70–90% of samples all end up as extreme standardized values. At n≈110 a few of these points get too much pull on the L2 logistic weights. I'm winsorizing the standardized features at ±3 SD, using limits from the training fold only, in both logistic members (whole-proteome and panel). That should cap the influence of outlying samples while keeping the rank order of each protein.

The panel logistic model now constrains each coefficient's sign to match its known direction in AD. It is fitted with L-BFGS-B and the same L2 penalty and C=0.1, with directions fixed in advance: tau, 14-3-3, SMOC1, neuroaxonal, glial and glycolytic proteins rise; neuronal pentraxins, VGF and secretory-granule proteins fall. Rounds 12–13 showed that fixed-direction scores are more stable at n≈110. This change applies the same idea inside the learned panel model, so it can still weight proteins but cannot flip a protein to the wrong direction because of noise in a small fold.
